entry.title: How ClamAV Works: Inside the Open-Source Antivirus Engine

link.title: How ClamAV Works: Inside the Open-Source Antivirus Engine

entry.content:
Watch clamd for a minute and you get a puzzle worth solving. The daemon sits on hundreds of megabytes of loaded signatures, yet a mail attachment is scanned, typed, decompressed, and matched before your IMAP client finishes repainting. The naive mental model — grep every signature against every file byte — predicts the opposite. Something about the data structures is fundamentally different.

ClamAV never searches for signatures at scan time in the naive sense. Loading a database is compilation: text lines are parsed once and baked into deterministic automata, and scanning is just execution against those automata. The scan itself is not one pass but a loop — detect the file type, dispatch to a parser, extract the children, and re-enter the same loop for each extracted layer until limits stop it.

This tour walks the main branch of Cisco-Talos/clamav end to end; every claim is a file-and-line citation on GitHub. We follow one file from cl_scanfile() through type detection, parser dispatch, and the match tiers; then how clamd multiplexes scans over a bounded thread pool; then the build facts that make the engine unusual. Neighboring design space: our tours of YARA and Suricata.

ClamAV's flow from clients to verdict: one accept thread feeds a bounded worker pool, every scan funnels through cli_magic_scan(), and all pattern work converges on matcher_run() over compiled tries.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • scanmanager() at manager.c, L1332 is the CLI path: cl_load() at manager.c, L1631 reads the database, cl_engine_compile() at manager.c, L1659 builds the tries — all in-process, no daemon needed.
  • main() at clamd.c, L144 does the same load-and-compile once at startup (clamd.c, L718, L752) and then serves clients forever.
  • tcpserver() at tcpserver.c, L52 binds the listening sockets, and acceptloop_th() at server-th.c, L519 is a single thread that accepts connections and buffers command data.
  • execute_or_dispatch_command() at session.c, L528 maps protocol verbs to work; thrmgr_new() at thrmgr.c, L695 created the pool those jobs land in.
  • Worker threads run scanner_thread() at server-th.c, L102, reaching cl_scanfile_callback() at scanner.c, L286 — the bridge into the engine.
  • cl_scanfile() at scanners.c, L6692 maps the file and enters cli_magic_scan() at scanners.c, L4724, the per-layer brain.
  • cli_determine_fmap_type() at filetypes.c, L331 decides what the file is, and switch (type) at scanners.c, L4966 decides which parser gets it.
  • cli_scan_fmap() at matcher.c, L1058 hands every chunk to matcher_run() at matcher.c, L99, where filter, Boyer-Moore, and Aho-Corasick tiers run in order.
  • updatedb() at libfreshclam_internal.c, L2360 keeps the database current — incrementally, as shown below.

The detailed view: 34 verified symbols from database loading to verdict, including the cache short-circuit, the MULTISCAN fan-out, and the four match tiers inside matcher_run().

Signature loading: from database lines to automata

The first architectural insight is that the database is code. cl_load() at readdb.c, L5373 walks the database directory, and cli_load() at readdb.c, L4829 picks a parser per file extension: .ndb goes to cli_loadndb() at readdb.c, L1685, .hdb/.hsb to cli_loadmd() at readdb.c, L3008, .ftm to cli_loadftm() at readdb.c, L2520, and .cdb container rules to readdb.c, L4961.

Byte-pattern lines from .ndb reach cli_add_content_match_pattern() at readdb.c, L754, which expands the wildcard syntax — {n} jumps, (a|b) alternations — and registers each part through cli_ac_addsig() at readdb.c, L872 into the Aho-Corasick trie, plus cli_bm_addpatt() at readdb.c, L1017 into the Boyer-Moore tables. Hash signatures take a different route: they land in the hm_hdb/hm_mdb/hm_imp/hm_fp matchers declared in the engine struct at others.h, L301, and a verdict becomes a digest lookup via cli_hm_scan() at matcher-hash.c, L403 — constant-time, regardless of how many hashes you have. ClamAV even accepts YARA rules: .yar/.yara files are dispatched at readdb.c, L4863, so signatures written in YARA syntax load into the same engine — our YARA tour explains what those rules compile into on their own.

The compile step is explicit and centralized. cl_engine_compile() at readdb.c, L6046 loops over every target-type matcher at readdb.c, L6126, calling cli_ac_buildtrie() at readdb.c, L6128 to stitch the trie’s failure links, then cli_pcre_build() at readdb.c, L6132 for regex signatures. A debug line at readdb.c, L6136 logs the per-matcher signature counts. Only after CL_DB_COMPILED is set at readdb.c, L6208 will any scan run — cli_magic_scan() refuses otherwise at scanners.c, L4744. Compile once, match many: the same reason CPython compiles source to bytecode before the interpreter loop starts.

The scan loop: type detection decides everything

cl_scanfile() at scanners.c, L6692 enters scan_common() at scanners.c, L5901, which funnels into cli_magic_scan() at scanners.c, L4724 — and this function runs once per layer, not once per file. Three gates run before any pattern matching. Size limits are enforced at scanners.c, L4756 against maxfilesize/maxscansize fields held in the engine struct at others.h, L279. The clean-file cache is consulted at scanners.c, L4896: clean_cache_check() at cache.c, L781 hashes the layer and, on a hit, ends the scan early at scanners.c, L4900 — previously-clean files pay one SHA-2 computation. Clean verdicts are recorded afterwards by clean_cache_add() at cache.c, L652.

Then comes typing: cli_determine_fmap_type() at filetypes.c, L331 matches magic bytes through the compiled .ftm table (cli_compare_ftm_file() at filetypes.c, L262) and through the same Aho-Corasick machinery running in filetype mode at filetypes.c, L472 — the trie is used for type detection too, not just virus matching. The result feeds switch (type) at scanners.c, L4966: one case per cli_file_t, each gated by dynamic-configuration flags that can disable whole parser families. A ZIP drops into cli_unzip() at scanners.c, L5063 (implemented at unzip.c, L1785); a RAR goes to cli_scanrar() at scanners.c, L522, gated on have_rar at scanners.c, L5002 because the unrar backend is an optional build.

Every extracted child re-enters the loop through cli_magic_scan_nested_fmap_type() at scanners.c, L5769 — recursion, bounded by max_recursion_level in the same engine limits. Types without a parser fall back to scanraw() at scanners.c, L3625, which matches the undecoded bytes directly. The insight: the parser tree is the scanner. A verdict is the union of pattern hits over every layer a file decompresses into, and the recursion limits are what keep nested archives tractable.

Four match tiers inside matcher_run

Pattern work converges on matcher_run() at matcher.c, L99, and its tier order explains the millisecond verdicts. Tier zero is the filter: filter_search_ext() at filtering.c, L734 — marked __hot__ in the source — consults a select/select-not structure built by filter_add_static() at filtering.c, L186 during load, and skips chunks no signature could match before any automaton runs.

Tier one is Boyer-Moore: cli_bm_scanbuff() at matcher.c, L149 (implemented at matcher-bm.c, L246) runs only when the engine isn’t in ac_only mode, handling signatures with relative-offset tokens. Tier two is the workhorse: cli_ac_scanbuff() at matcher.c, L164, the Aho-Corasick automaton at matcher-ac.c, L1981, which advances one state per input byte across all signatures simultaneously — this is the same multi-pattern family that Suricata uses for its fast-pattern matching, scaled down to files instead of packets. The final tiers live in the same function: image fuzzy-hash verification for graphics types at matcher.c, L188, and PCRE execution at matcher.c, L207 via cli_pcre_scanbuf() at matcher-pcre.c, L544.

The comment at matcher.c, L204 says it plainly: PCREs cannot run incrementally, so the tier re-checks PCRE_MAX_FILESIZE at matcher.c, L214 and loads the whole map into memory at matcher.c, L225 before executing regexes. AC/BM stream; regexes materialize. Repeatable insight: cheap deterministic tiers gate expensive expressive ones.

clamd: one accept thread, a bounded worker pool

The daemon’s shape is deliberate. main() at clamd.c, L144 compiles the engine exactly once, then acceptloop_th() at server-th.c, L519 — one thread — handles every socket: accept, read commands, parse_dispatch_cmd() at server-th.c, L676. The command table at session.c, L94 defines SCAN, INSTREAM, MULTISCAN and friends; execute_or_dispatch_command() at session.c, L528 turns each into a pool job via thrmgr_group_dispatch() at thrmgr.c, L1172.

The pool itself, created by thrmgr_new() at thrmgr.c, L695, grows lazily — thrmgr_dispatch_internal() at thrmgr.c, L1101 spawns a worker with pthread_create() at thrmgr.c, L1149 only when none are idle, up to the MaxThreads cap. Workers pop queued jobs and head for the engine. MULTISCAN is the clever bit: for a directory, the scan task at scanner.c, L236 fans out one job per file through the same pool (scanner.c, L263), and the budget check at session.c, L239 reserves one control thread so the client connection never starves. Database reloads swap the whole engine under running scans via reload_db() at server-th.c, L306. Shape to remember: I/O never waits on a scan; scans never run unbounded in parallel.

From C90 to Rust: build facts

The top-level CMakeLists.txt, L5 requires CMake 3.17, and — notable — CMakeLists.txt, L7 pins CMAKE_C_STANDARD to 90: the entire scan engine compiles as C90, a portability constraint inherited from decades of legacy Unix targets. The project version on main is 1.6.0 at CMakeLists.txt, L22, and libtool-style versioning yields libclamav.so.14 (CMakeLists.txt, L36).

Two toolchains coexist. Flex and Bison are hard requirements at CMakeLists.txt, L132 — and they exist for exactly one thing: generating the embedded YARA parser from yara_grammar.y/yara_lexer.l at libclamav/CMakeLists.txt, L115. Rust is equally required at CMakeLists.txt, L138: the workspace’s single crate libclamav_rust (edition 2021) brings DCT-based image fuzzy hashing via rustdct (fuzzy_hash.rs, L35), OneNote parsing from Talos’s forked onenote.rs, and the clam-sigutil signature toolkit — the modern parsers arriving as Rust FFI callbacks while the C90 core keeps the hot paths. Updates are incremental by design: updatedb() at libfreshclam_internal.c, L2360 fetches only the remote CVD header at libfreshclam_internal.c, L853, applies CDIFF patches at libfreshclam_internal.c, L1699, and rebuilds a compact .cld at libfreshclam_internal.c, L1879. One branch note: the default branch is main — the project moved from master, so older cloned paths on GitHub 404.

Honest Limits

Three caveats, each verifiable in the tree. First, this tour describes the engine, not detection quality: the repo ships the loader, matchers, and parsers — the live signature sets are Talos’s ongoing work distributed as CVD/CDIFF updates — so nothing here claims anything about what ClamAV detects today. Second, format support is build-conditional: the RAR path is gated on have_rar at scanners.c, L5002 and lives in the separately versioned libclamunrar/libclamunrar_iface trees, and the dynamic-configuration flags behind every switch (type) case let packagers or operators disable parser families outright — your binary may parse fewer formats than the source suggests. Third, memory behavior depends on compile options: the engine allocates its trie structures through a pool only when built with USE_MPOOL (others.c, L515, pointer at others.h, L351), and the PCRE tier can pull a whole file map into memory at matcher.c, L225 — so RAM and latency profiles vary by flags and signature mix, not architecture alone. Line numbers reflect main at the time of writing and will drift as commits land.
entry.summary: How ClamAV works: signature databases compile into Aho-Corasick tries, file type detection drives archive recursion, and clamd fans scans across threads.

entry.title: How hashcat Works: Inside the GPU Password Cracking Engine

link.title: How hashcat Works: Inside the GPU Password Cracking Engine

entry.content:
You run hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 ntlm.txt wordlist.txt on a laptop and the status line reports millions of guesses per second, while a homegrown Python cracker on the same machine manages a few thousand. The gap is not just “the GPU is fast.” It comes from a specific arrangement: candidates never leave the graphics card until they are hashed, one small kernel file per hash type is compiled by the driver at runtime, and a rule file that looks like extra work is actually an amplifier the hardware multiplies by. Where those gigahashes come from — and why a 40,000-line rule file costs exactly the rule count in extra time rather than a crawl — the source answers both.

The repository is easy to get lost in: over 1,300 kernel files under OpenCL/, hundreds of plugin sources under src/modules/, and a backend layer that hides the actual launches. This tour follows one candidate from wordlist.txt through the host scheduler into an OpenCL kernel and out to the crack printout, using only symbols and line numbers you can open yourself on master. The two diagrams below come from the same commit, so every node links back to its file.

Along the way you will meet the same dynamic-plugin pattern as YARA, whose modules extend the matcher at runtime — and if you read the earlier tour of the ClamAV scan engine, the split between “one dispatcher, many scanners” here will feel familiar. Hashcat pushes the pattern further: even the candidate producers and the low-level device bridges are runtime-loaded plugins, and one optional hash mode is itself written in Rust, a toolchain choice we covered separately.

Overview: from console entry to kernel launch. Feed plugins and dispatch threads sit between the attack modes and the backend that actually compiles and launches the OpenCL kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • int main is a thin shell: it hardens the dynamic-library search path, allocates the master context, and hands control to the session layer — see main, L2205.
  • hashcat_session_execute is the outermost driver: autodetect, module load, attack contexts, then rounds until the keyspace is exhausted or every hash is cracked — hashcat_session_execute, L3034. The per-round work loop is inner2_loop, L252.
  • straight_ctx_init sets up the -a 0 rule context — one no-op rule when you passed no -r, else a parse of your rule files — straight_ctx_init, L690, with the NOP rule materialized at straight_ctx_init, L716.
  • The mode plugin is opened by name: module_load dlopens modules/module_%05d.so built from the -m number — module_load, L149 and the path format at module_filename, L34.
  • Candidates come from feed plugins, not a hardcoded wordlist loop: the loader builds a feeds/<name>.so path and binds global_init/thread_next hooks — generic_session_load, L57, with the wordlist producer’s thread_next at thread_next, L77.
  • One worker thread per device packs batches and drives launches: thread_calc — thread_calc, L1749 — and fill_generic compresses candidates into the batch buffers — fill_generic, L794.
  • choose_kernel picks the kernel stages this batch needs, run_kernel performs the launch — choose_kernel, L2519 and run_kernel, L4068. Rule and mask amplifier passes go through run_kernel_amp, L5128.
  • The kernel file name comes from the plugin’s KERN_TYPE: the backend formats OpenCL/m%05d_a0-optimized.cl from it — kernel_filename, L1939. The GPU driver, not the build, compiles it at first use.
  • Two-dictionary (-a 1) attacks and their mask hybrids (-a 6, -a 7) share one wiring entry — combinator_ctx_init, L67.

Detail view: the full cast. Note how the module plugin (lower right) decides which kernel file gets loaded, and how the monitor and status layers only read from the launch path — they never sit inside it.

One candidate’s trip from wordlist.txt to the crack line

Follow hashcat -m 0 -a 0 -r rules/dive.rule on a plain MD5 list. The feed’s producer thread pulls one base word per call into an in-memory batch (thread_next, L77; a restore jump uses thread_seek at thread_seek, L84). fill_generic appends candidates to a pw_batch_t through pw_add, length-sorting into the device’s compressed candidate buffer (fill_generic, L794, pw_add call, L515). What reaches the GPU is compressed words in a flat u32 array (size_pws_comp, L2155), not char* strings.

The batch enters choose_kernel, which picks the launch shape. For fast hashes like MD5 the optimized shape is entered per password length: the comment above spells it out — kernel one is m00000_s04 up to 16 bytes, _s08 up to 32, _s16 beyond; the pure shape uses one kernel for all lengths (choose_kernel, L2519 with the mapping comment at kernel shape comment, L2501). run_kernel then launches at the autotuned work-group size (run_kernel, L4068). Inside m00000_s04, each work item rebuilds its candidate, computes MD5, and compares against the target digest words loaded from digests_buf into a search[4] array (m00000_s04, L148, digest load at digest load, L176). For raw MD5 the comparison happens inside the kernel itself; the module advertises this with ATTACK_EXEC = ATTACK_EXEC_INSIDE_KERNEL (module_00000.c, L14, constant at types.h, L900) — no per-candidate round trip to the host.

Only matches come back: the host calls check_hash per hit, which rebuilds the plaintext, writes the hash:plain line through outfile_write, emits the crack event, and appends the pair to the potfile (check_hash, L1806, outfile_write, L825, event emission at hashes.c, L2002, potfile append at potfile_write_append, L254). That asymmetry — millions of candidates flow down, a handful of hits flow up — is the whole trick. Slow-hash modes invert part of it: their KERN_RUN chains (types.h, L446 lists KERN_RUN_1 through KERN_RUN_AUX6) run init/loop/final stages with intermediate state copied back and forth per iteration, which is why Argon2 or bcrypt modes report thousands of H/s where MD5 reports millions.

Mode numbers are file names

The -m 0 number does triple duty, and once you see it the tree stops being intimidating. First it names the plugin: modules/module_00000.so (module_filename, L34). Second, the plugin declares everything the backend needs without any central registry: module_00000.c pins KERN_TYPE = 0 (module_00000.c, L23), the optimizer flags it wants (module_00000.c, L24), and its decode/encode hooks (module_init, L113). Third, KERN_TYPE becomes the kernel file name: the backend formats OpenCL/m%05d_a0-optimized.cl from it (kernel_filename, L1939), so -m 0 loads m00000_*.cl, and the -O switch picks optimized versus pure kernels (optimized path, L1956, pure path at pure path, L1974).

The consequence: adding a hash type means adding one module source plus its kernel file, nothing to register anywhere — src/modules/ holds 776 module_*.c sources and OpenCL/ carries 1,434 .cl files, 1,321 of them mode kernels. Compare the YARA tour’s shape: its modules extend the matcher from inside the scanning process, while each .so here is isolated behind a fixed ABI of hooks — module_hash_decode, module_hash_encode, and friends — so a broken plugin cannot drag the core down. Bridges for FPGA and Python-based modes (bridge_load, L49) reuse the same dynamic-loading idea one level further out.

Why a rule file multiplies throughput instead of halving it

The counterintuitive part is that a shipped ruleset like dive.rule — or a hand-built 40,000-line one — does not cost you a pass over the wordlist. straight_ctx_init loads your rules into a kernel_rule_t array (kernel_rules_load call, L728), and that array is shipped to the device as a kernel argument held in constant memory — the kernel-side declaration says exactly that: const kernel_rule_t *rules_buf (inc_common.h, L59), with the constant-memory note at inc_common.h, L15. The attack then reports its total as base words multiplied by the rule count: the amplifier arithmetic sits in one place, amplifier = straight_ctx->kernel_rules_cnt (amplifier, L462).

Because the rules live on the GPU and are applied per work item inside the kernel, the host never materializes a single word + rule pair. On the device the chain is: base word from the compressed buffer, rule expansion in registers, hash, compare. One launch covers words_per_item x rules_per_word candidates while uploading only the words. When the attack needs a separate expansion pass, it goes through run_kernel_amp (run_kernel_amp, L5128), backed by the amp kernel (amp, L16). This is also why progress reporting multiplies explicitly rather than reading a counter: with rules applied inside the engine, the total is dev_total x kernel_rules_cnt (words_total, L520).

The host scheduler and its one-second watchdog

The host side is deliberately boring, which is why it scales. thread_calc is spawned once per backend device (thread_calc, L1749), each thread asks get_work for a slice of the remaining keyspace sized to its device’s tuned kernel power (get_work, L202), fills a batch, launches, collects hits, repeats. Batches travel through slot buffers, so the producer runs concurrently with launches.

While that runs, one monitor thread wakes every second and does all the bookkeeping in a single place — temperature checks, runtime limits, restore checkpoints, status refreshes (monitor, L44, with the 1-second sleep_time at monitor.c, L63). The H/s line is aggregated by status_get_hashes_msec_all (status.c, L2227), and the live “Guess Candidates” column reads the device buffers via status_get_guess_candidates_dev, L1093. The banner and prompt live separately in welcome_screen, L179. Nothing in the monitor or status layer sits between a candidate and its kernel launch — in the detail diagram those nodes have edges to the launch path, not through it.

From make clean to a binary plus 776 plugins: build facts

The root Makefile is one line including src/Makefile, and its opening comment is the best architecture summary in the tree: a build produces four kinds of thing — the core as a shared library, a small frontend, the plugins (modules, bridges, feeds), and the kernels under OpenCL/, which are deliberately not compiled at build time because the GPU driver compiles them when hashcat runs (src/Makefile, L9). make clean && make produces libhashcat.so.8 plus the binary and every plugin (BUILD.md, L37). The release version stamped into the build is v8.0.0 (PRODUCTION_VERSION, L31). Windows defaults to the static arrangement (SHARED=0) while Linux/macOS default to the shared core (platform switch, L76).

Two optional modes bend the “just a C compiler” rule: mode 74000 wants Rust 1.85 or newer (BUILD.md, L15) and a build without it skips that mode cleanly; mode 73000 starts python3 at runtime instead of linking anything (BUILD.md, L17). Dependencies are vendored in-tree under deps/ (OpenCL headers, sse2neon, Argon2), so a fresh clone fetches no packages. One drift: the same Makefile comment still says “the 595 modules,” while the directory holds 776 module_*.c sources on the commit this post is pinned to — count them yourself if you reproduce this.

Honest Limits

  • Every line number here is pinned to master commit 1c1a305 (tree dated 2026-11-13). Master moves daily; if a symbol has moved, re-derive from the tree rather than trusting any anchor.
  • The tree contradicts its own docs in places — the 595-versus-776 module count above is one instance. Treat in-code comments as intent, not measurement.
  • The only concrete performance figure in the source is an anecdote in a comment — a launch-thread change that cost 411 ms per launch on an RTX 4090 versus 26 ms for the copy it sits in (types.h, L1682). Do not generalize it to your hardware; nothing in the repo publishes per-GPU throughput tables.
  • This tour describes the v8-era layout: src/feeds/, src/bridges/, and libhashcat.so do not exist in older tagged releases, so guides written against v6 or v7 will name different files for the same jobs.
  • Not every mode builds everywhere: the Rust-required mode is skipped without a toolchain, and BUILD.md’s platform matrix does not claim a full build on every OS.
entry.summary: How hashcat works inside: trace a wordlist candidate through OpenCL kernels, mode plugins, and rule amplifiers to the crack printout on one GPU.

entry.title: How Nmap Works: Inside the Source Code of the World’s Most Famous Port Scanner

link.title: How Nmap Works: Inside the Source Code of the World’s Most Famous Port Scanner

entry.content:
You run nmap -sV -sC against a /24 and thirty seconds later the terminal prints open ports, product names, and script findings for hundreds of hosts. Nothing in that output was hardcoded. No engineer sat down and wrote “probe 443 first, then 80.” One function and one loop decided every packet: which port, in what order, at what rate, with how many retries. That function is ultra_scan in scan_engine.cc, and once you have read it, every flag on the Nmap man page turns into a parameter you can explain.

The frustration that drives people into the source is always the same trio of symptoms: a port reports open|filtered on one host and plain filtered on the next; version detection prints http? where a browser sees nginx; a script fires on host A but not on the identical host B. Guessing fixes none of this, because the answers are state transitions inside C++ objects, not configuration knobs. You have to see the objects.

So we cloned nmap/nmap at master — commit 68739db8e4ec, checked out on 2026-11-14 — and followed that one command from argv to report. Every symbol below links to the file and line it occupies today, so you can verify any claim in two clicks. The tour deliberately sticks to the scanning core: targeting, the probe engine, the port state store, version detection, OS fingerprinting, and the script engine.

Nmap's master loop: nmap_main sequences targeting, the probe engine, detection passes, and three NSE script phases around a shared port-state store.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • nmap_main, L1862 parses every option, then runs a master loop that fetches host groups and executes each scan phase against them.
  • -T0..-T5 parsing, L1376 shows that timing templates are just preset assignments: T0 sets scan_delay to 300000 ms at L1381, T4 allows six retransmissions at L1402, T5 cuts that to two at L1412.
  • HostGroupState, L324 batches targets, and get_next_host, L452 yields each group’s hosts while skipping excluded ones.
  • getpts, L129 turns -p expressions into the scan_lists structure the engine consumes.
  • ultra_scan, L2735 is the single scheduler behind SYN, UDP, ACK and every other port scan; nmap_main calls it once per selected type starting at L2236.
  • UltraProbe, L153 is one schedulable probe of type UP_IP, UP_CONNECT, UP_ARP or UP_ND, sent through send_ip_packet, L411.
  • PortList::setPortState, L459 records the open/closed/filtered verdicts, and statenum2str, L941 renders exactly the strings you see in output.
  • After port scans, service_scan, L2790 and OSScan::os_scan, L3519 enrich the results, while open_nse, L940 has already booted the Lua VM for script phases.

The detail view: inside ultra_scan's probe loop, the version-detection queues, the OS fingerprint chain, and the Lua coroutine scheduler that NSE scripts live in.

One loop in nmap.cc decides the order of everything

nmap_main (nmap.cc, L1862) is where coordination lives. Two early lines are the most surprising in the whole file: when you pass -sV, the code sets o.scriptversion = true at L2101, and that flag alone triggers open_nse() at L2104. Version detection and the scripting engine are coupled from the very start — NSE’s Lua VM is booted before the first probe flies, even when you never typed --script.

Then the master loop runs the phases in fixed order per host group: each requested scan type through ultra_scan (L2236 through L2269, covering SYN, ACK, Window, FIN, Xmas, Null, Maimon, UDP, connect, SCTP and protocol scans), then service_scan at L2293, then OS detection at L2298, then the main script pass at L2307 and a post-scan pass at L2368. The pre-scan script phase ran even earlier, at L2110. Scripts therefore execute three separate times against the same target set — prerule, hostrule/portrule, postrule. Idle and FTP-bounce scans are the exceptions; the comment at L2271 admits they “can only handle one target at a time.”

ultra_scan is one scheduler, not thirteen

Every port scan type funnels into one function: void ultra_scan(std::vector<Target *> &Targets, const struct scan_lists *ports, stype scantype, struct timeout_info *to) at scan_engine.cc, L2735. It builds an UltraScanInfo at L2753 holding all per-host and global state, then calls begin_sniffer at L2780 only for raw scans. That conditional is why -sT (connect scan) works without root privileges: no pcap needed, replies arrive on real sockets.

The heartbeat is the loop at L2784: doAnyPings, doAnyOutstandingRetransmits, doAnyRetryStackRetransmits, then doAnyNewProbes (L2789–L2794). The order is deliberate — the source comments that retry-stack retransmits run after outstanding ones “for memory consumption reasons.” Retransmission is capped per probe: the check at L701 only allows another resend while probe->get_tryno() < maxval.

Pacing is not a sleep loop. ultra_timing_vals::ack and drop (timing.cc, L221, L244) rescale the send rate on every response or timeout, using thresholds from scan_performance_vars::init at L267. The -T presets just seed this machinery: T0 means one probe at a time with a five-minute scan_delay (L1381); T4 sets an RTT window of 100–1250 ms and caps the TCP scan delay at 10 ms (L1396–L1399); T5 allows a fifteen-minute host timeout but only two retransmissions (L1408, L1412). Notably, UDP is deliberately excluded from scan-delay caps in both T4 and T5 — the comments at L1401 and L1411 cite ICMP rate limiting and unreliability.

The port state machine is six strings and one function

Everything Nmap prints about a port resolves through statenum2str (portlist.cc, L941): open, filtered, unfiltered, closed, open|filtered, closed|filtered, otherwise unknown. That is the entire user-visible vocabulary. PortList::setPortState (L459) records transitions and hands back the old state, which is how the engine knows whether a port flipped mid-scan.

open|filtered deserves the repeatable insight: it exists for probe types where silence is ambiguous. A TCP SYN to a closed port gets a RST back (closed); silence means either a firewall dropped it or the service never answers UDP — so UDP and protocol scans leave ports in the combined state. Service detection then writes over the record through PortList::setServiceProbeResults (L307), storing name, version and tunnel info, while addScriptResult (L377) hangs script output off the same port object. One store, three writers, exactly the strings you read on screen.

Version detection: 188 probes and three queues

service_scan (service_scan.cc, L2790) organizes work in a ServiceGroup (L207) with exactly three queues — services_finished, services_in_progress, services_remaining (L211–L213). Each open port gets a ServiceNFO (L111) tracking its pending probe list and collected responses. startNextProbe (L2104) fires from nsock callbacks, sending the next probe only when round-trip timing allows.

The probe menu comes from nmap-service-probes, a single 17,166-line database file containing 188 Probe definitions with the regex match lines that classify banners. When a match hits, results are stored back through setServiceProbeResults at L2734 and L2774. Because -sV also switched on scriptversion, NSE service scripts contribute their findings into the same record.

How NSE threads attach to the scan

open_nse (nse_main.cc, L940) enforces hard engineering constraints: it refuses to run on anything below Lua 5.4 (L956), caps total Lua allocations at 400 MB via AllocState(400 * 1024 * 1024) (L964), and installs a five-second per-thread interrupt timer (L967) so a runaway script cannot freeze the scan. Entry into script land is script_scan (L992), which pushes run_main (L1000) and calls it through lua_pcall with the targets vector passed as light userdata.

On the Lua side, main(hosts, scantype) (nse_main.lua, L1451) drives everything. get_chosen_scripts (L730) resolves -sC and --script specs against script.db. The threads_iters table (L1393) spawns one coroutine per matching rule: prerule threads for pre-scan, hostrule and portrule threads per host and per port at L1409 and L1418, postrule threads last. The portrule loop iterates cnse.ports(host) at L1416 — the very ports the state machine classified. The scheduler run(threads_iter) (L905) resumes coroutines as their sockets become ready. So -sC is not magic: it is a coroutine pool reading the same PortList your output is rendered from.

From configure.ac to a single binary

The top-level build is classic autotools: configure.ac plus aclocal.m4, config.guess, and Makefile.in generate the makefile, with RPM specs (nmap.spec.in, zenmap.spec.in) and a BSDmakefile alongside. The CMakeLists.txt files that exist in the tree live only inside the vendored dependency folders — libpcap, libpcre, libz, libssh2, libdnet-stripped — not at the root. Those dependencies default to vendored copies: configure.ac offers --with-libpcap=included and friends, documented as “Always use the version included with Nmap.” The Lua runtime itself is carried in-tree via nse_lua.h, with lpeg.c at the root for pattern matching.

Two build quirks we observed while touring. First, the repository is a 2,611-file monorepo: it carries ncat/, zenmap/, and 619 .nse scripts under scripts/ next to the scanner core. Second, the -T option parser opens with a deliberately obfuscated one-liner at nmap.cc, L1377 — pointer arithmetic that mangles the argument in place — before falling into the readable if/else chain quoted above. All line numbers in this post were verified against master at 68739db8e4ec on 2026-11-14.

If this way of reading systems appeals to you, three more pyshine tours pair naturally with it: Redis runs a similarly single-threaded event loop over a completely different data model; NATS shows what fan-out and flow control look like when the scheduler lives in the protocol; and Traefik is worth the opposite comparison — routing instead of probing, with the same obsession over who gets sent what, when.

Honest Limits

  • Every symbol and line number was verified against master at commit 68739db8e4ec (cloned 2026-11-14). They will drift as the project moves; re-derive from the current tree before quoting them in patches.
  • The tour covers the scanning core only. ncat/, zenmap/, and the 619 NSE scripts under scripts/ are substantial subsystems we did not read here.
  • No benchmark numbers appear because none were measured: every timing figure cited (300000 ms delay, 400 MB cap, five-second script timer) is a source constant, not a performance result.
  • The “one scheduler” claim covers the mainstream raw and connect scans. Idle scan and FTP bounce scan are separate single-target paths, flagged as such in the source at L2271.
  • The -sV → NSE coupling (L2101–L2104) means the clean phase diagram hides one edge: scriptversion scripts run during version detection. We flag it; we did not trace that sub-path line by line.
entry.summary: How Nmap works, traced through its real C++ source: the ultra_scan scheduler, port state machine, -T timing presets, version detection and NSE hooks.

entry.title: Osquery
entry.content:
You type select * from processes into the osquery shell and a few hundred rows stream back — PIDs, memory footprints, parent processes, command lines. Then you look for the database file you just queried. There isn’t one. No processes.db, no .sqlite file, nothing on disk that ever stored those rows. The query feels like SQLite, the results look like a table, and yet the data was scraped out of the kernel microseconds before it hit your terminal.

The confusion gets worse once you deploy osqueryd. Your config file lists queries with intervals like 3600 seconds, but they never fire at exactly the hour marks, and logs show them drifting. Meanwhile results appear on some TLS endpoint you configured weeks ago and promptly forgot about. Every one of those behaviors is a deliberate decision in the source tree, not magic.

This post walks the osquery repository (the master branch as of this writing, all line numbers verified against the tree) and follows one innocent-looking SQL statement from the shell prompt down to /proc, then back up into a shipped log record. Every claim below is anchored to a file and line you can open yourself.

Overview: the SQL front-end, the virtual-table bridge, spec-generated platform tables, and the config/scheduler/telemetry loop of osquery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process starts in startOsquery, L146, which builds an Initializer, L148 — one binary that decides whether it becomes a shell, a daemon, or both.
  • Daemon mode lands in startDaemon, L97, which eventually calls startScheduler, L108 to begin the schedule runloop.
  • Shell mode is startShell, L114; it ends in launchIntoShell, L138, where the virtual tables are attached to the shell’s in-memory SQLite instance.
  • All SQLite resources flow through SQLiteDBManager, L207, whose instances are plain sqlite3_open(":memory:") handles — see sqlite3_open, L336. There is no file, ever.
  • Onto that empty database, attachVirtualTables, L1227 attaches one SQLite module per table plugin, wiring the callback table at sqlite_module_map, L1109.
  • The planner hook xBestIndex, L728 and the scan hook xFilter, L873 are where your WHERE pid = 1234 becomes a constraint the table generator actually uses.
  • The rows themselves come from platform code like genProcesses, L587, bound to the schema by a single line in the spec file.
  • Everything the scheduler collects is handed to logString, L375, which forwards it to whatever logger plugin is active.

Detail view: the xCreate/xBestIndex/xFilter/xColumn callback chain, the spec-to-plugin build flow, and the scheduling/telemetry plumbing.

select * from processes Never Touches a Disk Table

osquery is not a database with monitoring features; it is a monitoring system wearing SQLite as a syntax layer. When SQLite resolves processes during query preparation, it does not open a file — it invokes the virtual table module that osquery registered for that name. The registration happens in attachTableInternal, L1135, which maps every table name to the same C callbacks.

The first callback, xCreate, L563, asks the table plugin registry for column metadata via a columns action (Registry::call, L585) and feeds the answer to sqlite3_declare_vtab (L600). That is the moment your .table spec file becomes something SQLite genuinely believes is a table — it even parses a generated CREATE TABLE statement for it.

Query planning is intercepted too. SQLite calls xBestIndex, L728 with every constraint in your WHERE clause; osquery assigns each usable constraint an index ID from an atomic counter (kConstraintIndexID, L64, assigned at L857) and stashes the operator/operand pair. When the scan starts, xFilter, L873 reconstructs those pairs into a QueryContext (L934 onward) — so where pid = 1234 never enumerates all processes; the generator receives the constraint. Each cell SQLite fetches comes from xColumn, L701, which pulls from a cursor (BaseCursor, L36) that either holds a materialized row set or drives a coroutine-style RowGenerator.

One more subtlety: table plugins can declare attributes(cacheable=True) — the processes table does (processes.table, L52) — and the scheduler then sets TablePlugin::kCacheStep per run, letting repeated scans inside one interval reuse results (isCached, L821).

A Real SQLite, Just Without Real Tables

Nothing about the SQL dialect is faked. osquery compiles in SQLite and treats it as a library: the SQLiteDBManager, L207 header states outright that it “should be the ONLY method for accessing SQLite resources”, handing out thread-local instances backed by :memory: databases (L336). Every fresh instance immediately gets the full set of virtual tables attached (attachVirtualTables call, L508).

The execution path is equally stock: user SQL goes through queryInternal, L644, a thin wrapper over SQLite prepare/step. Even the planner output you get from EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in the shell is produced by literally running that statement (L548).

The interactive shell explains the déjà vu you may feel using osqueryi: the prompts are the classic sqlite> strings (L260) and queries run through runQuery, L1821 — the code descends from SQLite’s own shell. We compared this embedding pattern against the engine’s internals in our separate source tour of SQLite; osquery is effectively that engine plus one unusual extension: tables that time-travel into the kernel on demand.

One Spec File, Three Operating Systems

The columns of processes are not hand-written C++. They start life as a declarative spec, specs/processes.table, L3: a table_name, a column list with types and docs, and the crucial line implementation(“system/processes@genProcesses”), L53 that binds the schema to a C++ function. Platform-specific columns are layered on via extended_schema blocks for WINDOWS, L32, DARWIN, L41, and LINUX, L48 — which is why processes shows cgroup_path only on Linux and translated (Rosetta) only on macOS.

At build time the CMake glue in generateNativeTables, L11 and generateForeignTables, L14 expands these specs into native and “foreign” (cross-platform schema-only) plugin code. The generator itself, gentable.py, is a Python program — the interpreter that runs it is a cousin of the one we dissected in our CPython source walk, though here it is used as a build tool, not a runtime.

The implementation line points at per-platform directories: osquery/tables/system/linux/, windows/, darwin/. The Linux generator genProcesses, L587 asks for the pid list honoring your constraints, then for each pid fills a row by reading procfs: cmdline from readProcCMDLine, L47, symlinks like exe and cwd via readProcLink, L94 (used at L510). The Windows and Darwin twins live in osquery/tables/system/windows/processes.cpp and osquery/tables/system/darwin/processes.cpp respectively. The same spec mechanism also powers the signature-scanning tables — specs/yara_file.table, specs/yara_process.table, and specs/yara_events.table — which we connect to in our YARA source tour.

From Bundled CMake to the osqueryd Binary

The build is as opinionated as the runtime. master refuses to even configure on old tooling: cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25), L8, and an in-source build is a hard FATAL_ERROR, L14. The compiler is pinned by policy — on POSIX platforms the build warns unless you are using Clang (L52-L62), and the language level is set to C++17 via target_compile_features(... cxx_std_17) in cmake/flags.cmake, L28.

Third-party dependencies are not downloaded ad hoc; importLibraries, L95 declares a curated list of bundled formulas — lz4, augeas, openssl, boost, bzip2, gflags, glog, googletest, zlib, libarchive, libaudit, libcryptsetup, libdevmapper, libgcrypt, libiptables, libmagic, librdkafka, librpm, libudev, linenoise-ng, lzma and popt (L96-L120) — built from source under libraries/cmake/. The Linux preset in CMakePresets.json additionally expects osquery’s own sysroot (/usr/local/osquery-toolchain) so that one artifact family works across distributions.

The shipped binary is assembled the odd-but-documented way: add_osquery_executable(osqueryd …), L48 compiles an empty source file, and the comment above it explains the trick — an empty executable that links a library carrying the whole world of dependencies, which keeps the linker happy without recompiling main for every tweak. What links in is explicit: the osquery_main target, L69 and its siblings pull plugins_remote_enroll_tlsenroll, TLS config plugins, and the RocksDB/SQLite database plugins, which is why a default build can enroll over HTTPS out of the box.

The One-Second Loop: Schedule, Watchdog, Shipping

Scheduled queries are not cron jobs. SchedulerRunner::start, L277 runs a loop whose clock ticks in whole seconds; on each tick it walks the schedule exposed by Config::get().scheduledQueries and fires any query whose splayed interval divides the current epoch second (L293). That modulo test is the entire scheduling algorithm — plus a startup_priority kick for first runs. Interval “splay” comes from the config layer: Pack::initialize, L122 applies a percentage jitter (schedule_splay_percent, L40, computed at L116) so a thousand machines never query at the same second, and pack discovery queries gate whether the pack runs at all (L160).

Each fired query goes through launchQuery, L120, records its status as a monitoring metric, and marks table caches with the epoch tick (L298-L299). Between queries the same loop refreshes decorators (L230), reloads the schedule if --schedule_reload says so (L243), and flushes logs (L263) — all inside one thread, which is why a long query delays your logging. Config sources themselves are refreshed periodically by ConfigRefreshRunner, L307, keeping the schedule hot without a daemon restart.

The process around the loop is guarded twice. The daemon actually runs as a parent plus worker; Watcher, L96 and WatcherRunner, L236 spawn the worker (createWorker, L277), enforce CPU/memory limits with getWorkerLimit, and respawn it when it dies — even the watcher itself has a babysitter in WatcherWatcherRunner::start, L777.

Results leave through two registries. Enrollment happens once, via EnrollPlugin::call, L149 reading the enroll secret and obtaining a node key (the plugin registry lives at L63); everything then rides TLSTransport, L61. Log records pass logString, L375, which dispatches to the active logger plugin (L392) — filesystem, TLS, Kafka, whatever your config selects.

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers are from master at the time of writing and will drift; the files will not.
  • We read the Linux processes implementation line by line; the Windows and Darwin generators were located and linked but not analyzed here, and platform differences beyond the spec-level extended_schema blocks are not covered.
  • Only one target is registered as an executable in the CMake we read — osqueryd — and the interactive shell is reached through startShell in the same sources; treat any packaging detail (like how osqueryi is provided on your platform) as outside what this repo reading proves.
  • The scheduler fires queries on whole-second modulo ticks; that makes intervals approximate under load, and the drift counter (schedule_max_drift) pauses the loop rather than catching up — it is not a cron replacement.
  • attributes(cacheable=True) caching is tied to scheduler ticks, so caching benefits exist only for scheduled runs, not ad hoc shell queries.
  • No performance numbers appear here because we measured nothing; every claim is structural, read from the code.
entry.summary: You type select * from processes into the osquery shell and a few hundred rows stream back — PIDs, memory footprints, parent processes, command lines. Then you look for the database file you just queried. There isn’t one. No processes.db, no .sqlite file, nothing on disk that ever stored those rows. The query feels like SQLite, the results look like a table, and yet the data was scraped out of the kernel microseconds before it hit your terminal.

entry.title: How sqlmap Works: Inside the SQL Injection Automation Engine

link.title: How sqlmap Works: Inside the SQL Injection Automation Engine

entry.content:
Your WAF is on, your app has forty parameters, and last quarter’s scanner report said “no injection found”. Then someone points sqlmap at one URL parameter and, within minutes, it lands on a working boolean oracle plus the exact prefix/suffix pair that the scanner never tried. That gap is not luck. It is a specific engineering decision: sqlmap never sends one clever payload — it sends a filtered cross-product of payload templates and boundary vectors, and it reads each response with a similarity engine that turns HTTP pages into true/false answers. If you defend applications, knowing how that decision engine works tells you exactly which request shapes your WAF will see, and why a parameterized query is the only fix that removes the attack surface instead of filtering it.

The numbers behind the loop are concrete. On the current master branch, six XML dictionaries define 367 technique tests (75 boolean, 92 error-based, 118 time-based, 38 stacked, 36 UNION, 8 inline), and a second XML file defines 54 boundary vectors — the prefixes and suffixes that must wrap a payload for it to survive real SQL context. The detection loop walks both lists, prunes the combinations three ways before spending a request, and stops exploring once a parameter is confirmed injectable. Nothing about it is opaque; every number above is greppable in the repository.

The repo is a flat Python tree: lib/controller/ decides what to test, lib/core/ composes payloads, lib/request/ reads verdicts, data/xml/ stores every dialect, and tamper/ holds 85 mutators. This tour walks that path with line-level links, as defensive engineering documentation — after reading it you can explain, in your own words, what each phase contributes and why your WAF sees thousands of near-identical requests during a scan.

Overview: the scan controller drives a payload×boundary cross-product; every forged probe crosses the request layer, where tamper scripts mutate it and a comparison engine turns the response into a verdict.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • [start, L346](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/controller/controller.py#L346) — the scan orchestrator in lib/controller/controller.py discovers parameters, calibrates dynamicity, then hands each candidate to the detection loop.
  • [heuristicCheckSqlInjection, L1122](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/controller/checks.py#L1122) — before any real payload, a random string containing exactly one single quote and one double quote is injected to see whether the backend throws DBMS errors or mangles casting.
  • [checkSqlInjection, L126](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/controller/checks.py#L126) — the core loop: pops one ordered test at a time, then cycles every boundary that survives filtering.
  • [loadBoundaries, L83](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/parse/payloads.py#L83) — parses data/xml/boundaries.xml into 54 vectors, each carrying prefix, suffix, parameter type, clause and where filters.
  • [loadPayloads, L104](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/parse/payloads.py#L104) — parses the six files under data/xml/payloads/ into test objects, ranked later by [getSortedInjectionTests, L3965](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/core/common.py#L3965).
  • [Agent.payload, L117](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/core/agent.py#L117) — the composer in lib/core/agent.py: substitutes the parameter value with the forged statement and applies per-boundary prefix/suffix plus the technique’s terminating comment.
  • [queryPage, L1202](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/request/connect.py#L1202) — every request flows through this classifier in lib/request/connect.py; at L1278 it runs the tamper chain over the payload right before sending.
  • [comparison, L57](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/request/comparison.py#L57) — the ratio-based page diff in lib/request/comparison.py that decides whether a response means “expression was true”.
  • [bisection, L302](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/techniques/blind/inference.py#L302), [unionTest, L402](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/techniques/union/test.py#L402) and [errorUse, L303](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/techniques/error/use.py#L303) — the three extraction engines that consume confirmed injections: character-by-character blind reads, UNION column resolution, and error-channel extraction.

Detail view: how the detection loop prunes boundaries, how verdicts are classified, and where each technique engine and tamper script sits in the request path.

367 tests × 54 boundaries: the pruned cross-product

The counterintuitive part of sqlmap’s design is that the payload dictionaries and the boundary dictionary are separate. A test in data/xml/payloads/boolean_blind.xml says “run this expression and expect a page that looks true”; it deliberately says nothing about the surrounding SQL context. A boundary in data/xml/boundaries.xml says “this prefix/suffix pair works when the parameter lands inside a quoted string or inside a numeric context”; it says nothing about what the expression does. Only the loop joins them.

That join happens inside checkSqlInjection and it is heavily pruned. The test list is ordered once by technique priority (lib/core/common.py, getSortedInjectionTests), then per parameter the boundary list is pre-sorted: digit-like values get boundaries without quotes first, alphabetic values get quoted boundaries first (lib/controller/checks.py, L135–142). For each test/boundary pair the loop skips a boundary if its level exceeds --level (L414), if the test’s clause tags do not intersect the boundary’s clause tags (L421–427), or if the where tags do not match (L433–439). The user’s --prefix/--suffix flags override the dictionary entirely (L447–449). Once one pair succeeds, the loop stops re-cycling boundaries for the following tests (L454–461) — which is why a scan against a confirmable injection is thousands of requests, but a scan against a truly robust parameter set is far fewer.

The takeaway for defenders: every request shape your WAF sees is a legitimate member of this cross-product, including structural variants — comment-terminated suffixes, paren-balanced prefixes — that exist because context, not cleverness, is what makes an injection work. Rules that block only “quote followed by OR” catch the shallowest slice.

The verdict engine: turning HTTP responses into true/false

Detection is only as good as the oracle that reads responses, and sqlmap ships several. Before any payload, heuristicCheckSqlInjection sends a random string whose alphabet guarantees exactly one ' and one " (L1140–1146 of lib/controller/checks.py). The page can answer with a parsed DBMS error (positive), a casting exception (the parameter coerces input), or nothing (negative).

For boolean detection, comparison() in lib/request/comparison.py computes a similarity ratio against the baseline, with dynamic regions (reflected values, random tokens) accounted for. [queryPage, L1202](https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/blob/master/lib/request/connect.py#L1202) wraps it: build request, run tamper chain, classify. Expressions from boolean_blind.xml drive extraction: lib/request/inject.py picks the fastest technique per query in getValue (L633), and blind reads go through _goInference (L99) into bisection (L302 of lib/techniques/blind/inference.py) — one request per bit, binary-searching character codes. For time-based techniques the same file switches comparison mode at L329 (timeBasedCompare for TIME and STACKED): instead of “does the page differ” it asks “did the response take as long as the payload’s SLEEP vector requested”, with vectors like MySQL’s BENCHMARK() and PostgreSQL’s pg_sleep() from time_blind.xml — see our MySQL and PostgreSQL source tours for why those two engines dominate the delay dictionary.

Two optimizations matter when you measure scan noise: lib/techniques/blind/multibit.py packs several bits into one request (attempt, L884), and lib/request/timeless.py compares fast/slow request pairs statistically (readBit, L176, calibrated at L217) for cases where a WAF rewrites every response body so page comparison is useless.

Dialect knowledge lives in XML, not Python

The single largest data file is data/xml/queries.xml — roughly 171 KB of per-DBMS SQL as <dbms> sections (MySQL first, then PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite and more): fingerprint, banner, delay, cast and limit syntax, all of it data. The same pattern holds for errors — data/xml/errors.xml matches each engine’s error pages, which is how heuristicCheckDbms (L925 of lib/controller/checks.py) guesses the backend from one quote-probe response; the loop then offers to narrow remaining tests to that engine (reduceTests, L184), because identifying MySQL early saves firing Oracle-specific payloads at every boundary.

Runtime dialect adjustments are code, but deliberately thin: plugins/dbms/<engine>/ ships one module per backend — for MySQL, syntax.py defines a Syntax class whose escape (L17) implements the engine’s escaping rules, with sibling modules for fingerprinting, enumeration and takeover. The error-based extractor shows the same economics: errorUse (L303 of lib/techniques/error/use.py) reuses whatever error channel the fingerprint found, through _oneShotErrorUse (L63), which asks the database to smuggle an entire query result into one error message. For defenders the patch list is the same: disable verbose errors, and the whole error-based family of 92 tests collapses.

Tamper scripts: the sanctioned mutation layer

The cross-product composes payloads from fixed dictionaries, but real WAFs need mutation that dictionaries cannot anticipate. sqlmap’s answer is the tamper layer: 85 scripts in tamper/, each a pure function with the same contract — def tamper(payload, **kwargs), plus an optional dependencies() (L13) and a __priority__ ordering constant (see tamper/space2comment.py, L11–16). The scripts are loaded at startup into kb.tamperFunctions (lib/core/option.py, L937), and at request time lib/request/connect.py runs the chain in order (L1278–1284), passing each function the payload, headers, parameter delimiter and a shared hints dict; a tamper that returns a non-string is rejected with an exception, and the engine warns when more than three tampers are stacked (L972).

space2comment is the minimal example: SELECT id FROM users becomes SELECT/**/id/**/FROM/**/users — spaces swap for inline comments, a form naive WAF regexes miss because the statement stays valid. The architectural insight: tampering is orthogonal to detection. The loop never knows what the tamper layer did to its payload; it only sees the verdict, which is why tamper scripts are a separate directory rather than options inside payload XML. For defenders, the directory doubles as a catalog of evasion shapes your rules should tolerate or normalize — and parameterized queries remove the surface that makes all 85 scripts relevant in the first place. One verified edge case: for non-SQL engines (the NoSQL/LDAP family in lib/techniques/), startup resets kb.tamperFunctions to empty (lib/core/option.py, L983–991), since SQL-comment mutation is meaningless there.

From git clone to running scan: what’s actually in the box

Build facts worth knowing before you vendor or audit this code. It is pure Python with no pip dependencies: the README states it “works out of the box with Python version 2.7 and 3.x”, and Python 2 compatibility lives in lib/core/compat.py (shims for cmp at L194, round at L226, cmp_to_key at L241) — tamper scripts even import xrange from it. External libraries are vendored under thirdparty/ (bottle, chardet, beautifulsoup), so a clone is self-contained; our CPython source tour covers the interpreter side that makes a single codebase run across both language versions. Entry points: sqlmap.py for the CLI, sqlmapapi.py for the REST API, with CI in .github/workflows/tests.yml.

Version identity is unusual: lib/core/settings.py sets VERSION = "1.10.11.88" (L22), where the trailing component is a build counter rather than a semver digit. Two layout quirks we hit while writing this tour: the project’s GitHub path is now sqlmapproject/sqlmap (the older sqlmap/sqlmap path currently 404s, and every citation link above uses the canonical path), and there is no lib/core/start.py — scan orchestration lives in lib/controller/controller.py, which surprises readers who memorized older layouts. The XML dictionaries are versioned alongside the code, so a WAF rule written against last year’s test list can silently miss this year’s.

Honest Limits

  • All counts (367 tests, 54 boundaries, 85 tamper scripts, the version string) are from the master branch at the time of writing; this project edits its dictionaries frequently, so re-grep before citing them.
  • Detection is not exploitation: many tests depend on observable side effects — verbose errors, reflected results, stable baselines — so hardened apps can be injection-free as far as the oracle can see, and “no injection found” is a weaker claim than it sounds.
  • Time-based detection inherits network noise: the engine classifies a slow response as a match, so latency variance on congested links produces false positives that must be re-verified with the confirmation logic in lib/techniques/blind/inference.py.
  • The page-comparison oracle needs a usable baseline: heavily dynamic pages degrade the similarity ratio, which is why the controller calibrates dynamicity before testing.
  • Tamper scripts mutate payloads but cannot make an incompatible statement valid — and they are disabled entirely for non-SQL engines (lib/core/option.py, L983–991), so scanning a NoSQL or LDAP backend with SQL tampers configured silently drops them.
entry.summary: How sqlmap finds SQL injection: 367 payload tests, 54 boundary vectors, boolean/time oracles, DBMS dialect XML and the tamper layer, explained from source.

entry.title: How Suricata Works: Inside the IDS Engine That Detects Attacks at Wire Speed

link.title: How Suricata Works: Inside the IDS Engine That Detects Attacks at Wire Speed

entry.content:
Suricata sits on the tap where your 10 Gbps uplink lands, and it has to reach a verdict on every packet that crosses that wire: alert, drop, or pass. Feed the engine the wrong threading configuration and the verdict happens in the wrong place — packets bounce between capture threads and detection threads through mutex-protected queues, and contention on those queues eats the throughput you bought the hardware for. The default autofp (“automatic flow pinning”) runmode still works that way, which is exactly why Suricata’s own configuration file tells you that 'workers' generally gives best performance (suricata.yaml.in, L1433).

The second pain point is the ruleset. A production deployment carries thousands of signatures, and evaluating every signature against every packet is hopeless — the math only works if you can discard 99.9% of the rules before inspecting a single payload byte. Suricata solves this at load time: it compiles each rule’s strongest content match into a multi-pattern matcher — Intel Hyperscan when built with --enable-hyperscan, its own Aho-Corasick implementation otherwise — and scans the whole pattern set in one pass per buffer.

This article reads the actual source in execution order, from main() to the alert log, and every file and line number below was verified against the main branch of OISF/suricata at commit c48ca372deb3 (version 9.0.0-dev). If you have followed our tours of Zeek and Wireshark, this completes the set: Zeek is the scriptable event engine, Wireshark is the deep decoder, and Suricata is the one that has to keep up with the wire while doing it.

Overview: one worker thread per rx queue runs the full capture → decode → detect → output chain inline. Diagram links point into the OISF/suricata repository on branch main.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L20 — int main(argc, argv) calls SuricataMainLoop(), which ends in RunModeDispatch (suricata.c, L3219).
  • RunModeDispatch, L404 — looks up the mode handler, calls it, then spawns management threads: FlowManagerThreadSpawn (L447) and StatsSpawnThreads (L452).
  • RunModeSetLiveCaptureWorkers, L329 — the workers-mode entry point; one thread per configured rx queue.
  • ReceiveAFPLoop, L1308 — the AF_PACKET ring read loop, slot 1 of the worker chain.
  • DecodeAFP, L2749 — slot 2, dispatching by datalink type into DecodeEthernet, L41.
  • FlowWorker, L563 — slot 3, the fused module that does flow lookup, TCP reassembly, detection and logging for the same packet.
  • Detect, L3281 — the detection entry, branching to DetectFlow when the packet belongs to a flow.
  • Prefilter, L244 — runs the precompiled MPM engines; SCHSSearch, L1063 is the Hyperscan variant.
  • OutputLoggerLog, L794 — flushes alerts and logs, still inside the same worker thread.

Detail view: the runtime packet path (top) plus the load-time rule compilation path that produces the match structures the prefilter scans.

One Thread Per Rx Queue: The Workers Runmode

When you set runmode: workers, RunModeDispatch ends up in RunModeSetLiveCaptureWorkersForDevice, L244, which loops once per thread: threads_count = MIN(ModThreadsCount(aconf), thread_max) (L256), capped by TmThreadsGetWorkerThreadMax() (L251). Each thread is created by TmThreadCreatePacketHandler with "packetpool" as both input and output handler and "pktacqloop" as its loop type (L282–285). The thread names tell you the model at a glance — "W" (runmodes.c, L67) formatted as W#01-eth0 (L278).

The interesting part is what gets attached to each thread. Four modules are appended as a fixed slot chain: the receive module (TmSlotSetFuncAppend, L299), the decode module (L305), "FlowWorker" (L307–311), and "RespondReject" (L313–317), before TmThreadSetCPU(tv, WORKER_CPU_SET) (L319) pins it and TmThreadSpawn (L321) starts it. The AF_PACKET case is wired in runmode-af-packet.c, L883, which passes "ReceiveAFP" and "DecodeAFP" as slots 1 and 2. The insight you can repeat later: in workers mode, a packet’s entire life — capture, decode, flow, detect, output — happens inside one thread, so the only cross-thread coordination left is the flow hash itself, a shared bucket table where FlowGetFlowFromHash, L903 computes hash % flow_config.hash_size (L909) and returns the flow locked. Flow assignment happens earlier via FlowSetupPacket, L528.

Contrast this with autofp: capture threads finish each packet by calling TmqhOutputFlowHash (tmqh-flow.c, L219) to pick a queue, and the detect thread pulls from it with TmqhInputFlow (L97), which sits inside SCMutexLock (L103) and SCCondWait (L106). Every packet pays at least two queue hops with real mutexes. The schedulers — hash, ippair, ftp-hash (L58–80) — only decide which queue; they cannot remove the hops.

No Queues in the Hot Path: Slot Chains and the Packet Pool

How does a packet move between the four slots of a worker without locking anything? It doesn’t move at all. ReceiveAFPLoop, L1308 reads the kernel ring (V2 or V3 TPACKET, chosen at L1323–1327) and hands the packet pointer straight to TmThreadsSlotProcessPkt (L1020), an inline function defined in tm-threads.h, L194. That calls TmThreadsSlotVarRun (tm-threads.c, L134), whose entire job is the loop for (TmSlot *s = slot; s != NULL; s = s->slot_next) — invoking each module’s SlotFunc on the same packet, in order, on the same stack (L136–138). Decode itself is slot 2: DecodeAFP (L2749 of source-af-packet.c) calls DecodeLinkLayer (L2762), which routes by datalink into DecodeEthernet — parse the 14-byte header, then dispatch on ethertype (decode-ethernet.c, L60) toward DecodeIPV4 (decode-ipv4.c, L515) and its protocol chain. The only “queue” on this path is for decode pseudo-packets — fragments, tunnels — handled by TmThreadsProcessDecodePseudoPackets over a PacketQueueNoLock (tm-threads.c, L115), which is safe because those packets stay private to the thread.

The other lock-avoidance trick is memory. Packet buffers come from a pool that is declared thread_local PktPool thread_pkt_pool (tmqh-packetpool.c, L44); PacketPoolInit (L235) preallocates max_pending_packets buffers per thread, and when a worker wants to lend a packet to a neighbor it only touches a shared return stack after crossing return_threshold of 32 (L247–248). Below the threshold, returns are batched and the shared mutex is never taken — the allocator never becomes a bottleneck in the hot loop.

From Rule String to Match Structure

Everything above is the runtime; now look at what happens at startup, because that is where thousands of rules become a data structure a thread can scan in one pass. Parsing lives in detect-parse.c: SigParse, L2238 turns alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 445 (...) into a Signature with option lists. Then RetrieveFPForSig, L1181 picks the signature’s fast pattern — the longest, most selective content — and registers it with the configured matcher. The algorithm comes from mpm-algo in suricata.yaml.in: auto uses "hs" if Hyperscan is available, "ac" otherwise (suricata.yaml.in, L1928, with mpm-algo: auto at L1938). Request hs on a build without it and startup dies: FatalError("Hyperscan (hs) support for mpm-algo is " ...) (detect-engine-mpm.c, L968).

Next, SigGroupBuild, L2300 partitions signatures into SigGroupHead groups by protocol, port and direction — this is why a packet to port 445 never sees the SSH rules. For each group, PrefilterAppendPayloadEngine, L349 binds an MPM engine instance whose pattern set contains exactly the fast patterns of that group’s signatures. Finally, per worker thread, PatternMatchThreadPrepare, L993 builds thread-private MPM contexts — for Hyperscan that means cloning a scratch region per thread, since hs_scan requires one and sharing it would be a race. The load-time result: at runtime, “run all rules” has already collapsed into “scan one per-group pattern database, get a short list of candidate signature IDs.”

What Actually Happens When a Rule Matches

Follow one packet through FlowWorker (flow-worker.c, L563). FlowHandlePacket (L585) attaches the flow — the comment at L596 reads “Flow is now LOCKED” — then for TCP, FlowWorkerStreamTCPUpdate (L645) feeds reassembled bytes into the app layer: AppLayerHandleTCPData (app-layer.c, L713) → AppLayerParserParse (app-layer-parser.c, L1528), the same parsing machinery that reconstructs HTTP, TLS, or the scan probes an nmap sweep generates. Then Detect runs (L664).

Inside DetectFlow, L3193, the first real work is not rule evaluation at all: DetectRunPrefilterPkt (L621) calls PacketCreateMask (L625) to mark what the packet contains, then Prefilter (L627). That runs the group’s MPM engine — SCHSSearch (util-mpm-hs.c, L1063) wraps hs_scan (L1082), and each match event calls PrefilterAddSids (L1045) to append candidate signature IDs to the thread’s pmq. If nothing matched, pmq.rule_id_array_cnt stays zero (L629 of detect.c) and detection is over — thousands of rules were “checked” without inspecting one payload. Otherwise DetectPrefilterCopyDeDup (L637) deduplicates the candidate list, and only those signatures proceed: a cheap header test per candidate via DetectRunInspectRuleHeader (L525), then full payload evaluation in DetectEngineContentInspection (detect-engine-content-inspection.c, L761) — offsets, depths, pcre, transforms. On a real match, AlertQueueAppendPacket (detect-engine-alert.c, L476) appends the alert to the packet’s queue (called from detect.c L3162), DetectRunPostMatch (L263) applies rule actions, and back in FlowWorker, OutputLoggerLog (L670) flushes it to whatever loggers registered at startup via OutputRegisterLoggers (output.c, L1079). The verdict was produced without the worker ever waiting on another worker.

From configure.ac to Suricata Binary

  • The main branch is mid-development of the next major release: AC_INIT([suricata],[9.0.0-dev]) (configure.ac, L1). Build with autogen.sh then configure && make; configure.ac demands pkg-config before anything else (L82).
  • Hard dependencies are modest: pcre2-8 (L627), libyaml (checked at L713), pthread (L774), zlib (L599), and — a recent change — Jansson is now mandatory, with the error message “Jansson is now required” (L807–814).
  • Hyperscan is optional and detected two ways: pkg-config first, then AC_CHECK_LIB(hs,hs_compile,,...), finally defining BUILD_HYPERSCAN (L655–692). Omit it and the engine silently falls back to Aho-Corasick (mpm-algo: auto).
  • The shipped configuration is a template: suricata.yaml.in gets its @VAR@ substitutions from configure, so config edits belong in the installed suricata.yaml.
  • One layout surprise: there is no runmode-workers.c. Workers logic lives in util-runmodes.c; each capture backend (pcap, af-packet, netmap, dpdk, …) has a thin runmode-*.c that just calls RunModeSetLiveCaptureWorkers with its own module names.
  • Branch quirk worth knowing when linking code: the default branch is main, not master, and this analysis is pinned to commit c48ca372deb3.

Honest Limits

  • Everything here is verified against main at commit c48ca372deb3 (9.0.0-dev). Suricata moves fast — line numbers will drift between releases, though the module names are stable.
  • The tour covers live AF_PACKET capture and the workers/autofp modes. Not covered: offline pcap processing, DPDK, Netmap, Af-XDP, eBPF load balancing, the unix-socket runmode, and IPS peering (the AFPPeersListCheck gate at runmode-af-packet.c, L890 enforces one peer per capture thread in inline mode).
  • “No lock in the hot path” is precise for the workers slot chain. It is not true globally: autofp genuinely takes mutexes per packet (tmqh-flow.c L103–106), and the packet-pool return stack takes a shared mutex once a thread’s lend balance crosses 32 (tmqh-packetpool.c L245–248). The flow hash buckets are also locked per bucket — briefly, but not never.
  • The 10 Gbps framing is the deployment scale Suricata is engineered for, not a benchmark we ran. Throughput depends on your ruleset, threads: auto under af-packet (suricata.yaml.in, L675), ring sizing, and hardware; measure with your own traffic.
  • The diagrams omit the management threads that RunModeDispatch spawns alongside workers — flow manager, flow recycler, stats (runmodes.c, L447) — since they sit outside the per-packet path.
entry.summary: How Suricata detects attacks at wire speed: worker threads, inline slot chains, Hyperscan MPM prefiltering, and what happens when a rule matches.

entry.title: How Wazuh Works: Inside the Agent-to-Engine Event Chain of the Open-Source SIEM

link.title: How Wazuh Works: Inside the Agent-to-Engine Event Chain of the Open-Source SIEM

entry.content:
It is 3:12 a.m. and your dashboard paints a red row: a file-integrity alert for /etc/passwd on a payment-subnet host. What actually happened between the realtime watcher that noticed the write and the JSON document you are now reading? In the Wazuh repository’s default main branch — version 5.1.0, stage alpha0 at the time of writing — the answer is a chain of five cooperating programs with one queue between each pair, and every link of that chain sits in source you can open today.

The chain is easy to misread from the outside. The agent looks like one black box that “sends logs”; the manager looks like one service that “makes alerts”. The source says otherwise. On the host, logcollector tails files, syscheckd diffs filesystems, and a shared message-queue helper frames every event into the same local socket. agentd forwards them; an HTTPS client batches, compresses and ships them. On the manager, remoted authenticates and forwards — it does not analyze. A separate engine process turns batches into classified events destined for the indexer, and the historical rule engine those alerts once flowed through is gone from this branch entirely.

This article follows one event end to end through the real code, not the marketing block diagram. Every claim below is anchored to a file and a line in wazuh/wazuh on its default branch, so you can click through and argue with the source.

Figure 1 — The Wazuh event chain from agent modules to the wazuh-indexer (wazuh/wazuh, main branch).

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SendMSGtoSCK, L2102 — logcollector hands each parsed line to the local queue through this one helper.
  • fim_send_msg, L521 — FIM wraps event emission here and ships via SendMSGPredicated at L526 with the SYSCHECK location.
  • SendMSGAction, L210 — the shared writer every module funnels through; OS_SendUnix delivers the framed datagram at L293.
  • EventForward, L30 — the only queue agentd drains; it strips the trailing NUL and submits at L51.
  • EventAccumulator, L45 — batching with drop-newest back-pressure when the cap is hit.
  • statelessStream target, L251 — the agent POSTs each batch to /stateless, opening the body with an H metadata line at L20.
  • statelessEndpoint target, L25 — the manager forwards to /events/enriched over a Unix socket and returns 202 at L49 once the engine enqueues.
  • pushEvent, L138 — the engine’s event API parses the NDJSON batch and posts each event to the router at L135.
  • Router::ingest, L205 — priority-table fan-out into matching policy environments at L219; the shipped output config indexer.yml, L19 names the destination streams.

Figure 2 — The same chain with internals exposed: queues, authentication, decompression, router workers, policy stages, and the stores behind them.

One queue, one forwarder, one transport

Every collecting module on the host writes to the same local Unix socket, and that is the whole agent-side architecture in one sentence. SendMSGAction, L210 is the shared writer: it frames a location character plus the message and hands the buffer to OS_SendUnix. FIM events arrive with the SYSCHECK location via fim_send_msg, log lines arrive through SendMSGtoSCK, rootcheck writes through the same helper family, and nothing in the modules knows what happens next. On the receiving end, wazuh-agentd opened DEFAULTQUEUE in read mode at startup (agentd.c, L229) and its monitor loop calls exactly one consumer, EventForward, at L335.

EventForward is deliberately dumb: a non-blocking recv loop (event-forward.c, L30) that increments a message counter, trims the trailing NUL that OS_SendUnix’s string convention attached (lines 37–49), and calls w_https_client_submit_event. Per-module routing has been deleted from the agent — the comment above notes sync sessions go straight to the module’s stream intake, so a single frame class remains.

The interesting decisions happen after the hand-off. agentd treats the HTTPS client as the agent’s only transport (agentd.c lines 264–268): it owns connection lifecycle, keepalives and buffering, and if it fails to start, the agent exits rather than run unreachable. Events accumulate in an accumulator whose append drops the newest event once the cap (capMultiplier x batchSize) is hit — drop-newest, not drop-oldest, so an overwhelmed agent sheds fresh data first. The stateless stream opens each request body with an H metadata line and POSTs to /stateless, logging Sending /stateless batch (%llu events, %zu bytes); a single event too large for the wire is dropped with its own warning. Enrollment runs before any of this: a token bootstrap that refuses to enroll unverified rather than fall through to the legacy path (agentd.c, L175), and identity keys loaded via OS_ReadKeys (L215), implemented in keys.c, L223.
